summary: Defines the structure of the RPKI distributed repository. Each publication point is a directory holding certificates, revocation lists and signed objects. It specifies naming of files, what each publication point contains, and a suggested layout for a local cache that helps with synchronizing.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines how RPKI certificates and signed objects are organized for public retrieval. It specifies what each publication point contains, how files are named and how relying parties can maintain a local copy.

subtitle: How the RPKI publishes certificates, revocation lists, manifests and signed objects.

tldr.problem: RPKI relying parties need predictable access to certificates, certificate revocation lists and signed objects in a distributed repository.
tldr.mechanism: Each certification authority publishes current objects at a publication point, with a manifest that lists their names and hashes. Relying parties can synchronize a local cache by walking the certificate hierarchy from their trust anchors.
tldr.outcome: The profile specifies repository contents, file extensions and synchronization guidance. It warns that repository contents and manifests may be temporarily inconsistent.

today: RFC 6481 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2012. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the repository profile used by related specifications including RFC 6486 and RFC 6487.

sections.title: Why the RPKI Uses Repositories
sections.content:
Relying parties need access to the resource certificates, certificate revocation lists (CRLs) and signed objects that make up the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI). Each issuer publishes objects in a repository so relying parties can retrieve them.

This profile recommends a common file-naming scheme, defines the contents of publication points and suggests how to organize a local cache. A repository object is a terminal item, usually a file. A publication point is a collection of objects, usually a directory identified by a URI.

A resource certificate binds a public key to IP address blocks and autonomous-system numbers. The subject can demonstrate control of those resources by signing with the matching private key.
sections.plainLanguage: Relying parties need to fetch the certificates and signed objects used by RPKI. This RFC defines a consistent way to publish those files and organize local copies.

sections.title: Publication Points and Certificate Links
sections.content:
The RPKI repository consists of multiple repository instances and publication points; one repository does not need to hold every object. Each certification authority (CA) has an authoritative publication point for its current certificates and CRLs.

The Subject Information Access (SIA) extension of a CA certificate points to the CA's publication point. The Authority Information Access (AIA) extension of a subordinate certificate points to the CA certificate under which it was issued. A certificate's CRL Distribution Points extension points to the relevant CRL.

Every publication point MUST contain a manifest. The manifest lists the names and hashes of the objects published there, excluding the manifest itself. A CA can make several directory changes before publishing a manifest that covers them.
sections.plainLanguage: Certificate fields point to the issuer's certificate, the issuer's publication directory and the relevant revocation list. Each directory also has a manifest listing its published objects.

sections.title: Files and Their Extensions
sections.content:
A CA publication point contains its current, non-expired and non-revoked certificates, its most recent CRL, its current manifest and signed objects validated by an end-entity certificate it issued.

  • .cer identifies a DER-encoded certificate; each file contains one certificate.
  • .crl identifies a DER-encoded CRL; each file contains one CRL, and a new CRL replaces the previous one.
  • .mft identifies a manifest; a new manifest replaces the previous one.
  • .roa identifies a Route Origin Authorization.

A series of certificates with the same subject, key and resources should share a filename so the newer certificate replaces the previous one. Signed objects must not use the certificate, CRL or manifest extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: File extensions identify certificates, CRLs, manifests and ROAs. New versions replace older files so a publication point contains current objects rather than old copies.

sections.title: Operating and Updating a Repository
sections.content:
The repository MUST be available using rsync. Operators may offer other retrieval methods if they match the access methods listed in certificate SIA fields. The RFC recommends a highly available, high-capacity publication service.

A publication point should contain the CA's products and appropriate subordinate publication points, not unrelated files. Operators should manage directory updates so relying parties are less likely to see intermediate states while objects and manifests change.

Even with careful updates, a repository may briefly disagree with its manifest. Relying parties should not assume that both are consistent at every moment.
sections.plainLanguage: Repositories must support rsync and should be available reliably. Updates should limit inconsistent views, but relying parties must allow for temporary mismatches between a directory and its manifest.

sections.title: Reissuing Certificates and Synchronizing a Cache
sections.content:
When a CA certificate is reissued, the CA should keep using the same publication point so subordinate certificates' AIA pointers remain valid. During key rollover, the same publication point may temporarily contain products from both CA instances; products from the new CA replace those from the old one.

For efficient validation, the RFC recommends that each relying party keep a synchronized local repository. Synchronization starts from locally selected trust anchors and recursively collects valid certificates issued by each CA. The traversal should enforce a maximum chain length so a loop in the hierarchy cannot cause a malfunction.

Relying parties should use manifests to check repository contents and account for temporary inconsistencies. The RFC gives examples such as synchronizing twice or fetching a manifest before and after retrieving a directory.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping publication-point names stable helps subordinate certificates continue to find their issuer's files. A local cache should start from trusted anchors, follow certificate links and check manifests for updates.

sections.title: Repository Security and Registrations
sections.content:
Repositories are not assumed to be integrity-protected databases, and retrieval may be exposed to man-in-the-middle attacks. Relying parties can detect corrupted objects by checking signatures, older object replacements through manifests, and revoked certificates by processing CRLs.

Manifests and CRLs do not detect every substitution of an older but still valid object. Repositories and signed objects also provide no confidentiality, so data that requires controlled access should not be published unless another specified mechanism protects it.

IANA registered the media types application/rpki-manifest and application/rpki-roa, and established a registry for repository filename extensions. Initial extensions are .cer, .crl, .mft and .roa.
sections.plainLanguage: Signatures, manifests and CRLs detect many repository changes, but they do not provide confidentiality or detect every old valid object. Do not publish controlled-access data without separate protection.

items.label: Certificate Revocation List
items.desc: One DER-encoded CRL per file; the latest replaces the previous one.

items.label: Manifest
items.desc: Lists object names and content hashes.
